title: Morning Edition
notes: It prioritizes developments since Saturday’s morning edition: SpaceX’s first catch of a Starship spacecraft, the government’s account of what caused Friday’s nationwide ground stop, Iran’s latest claimed drone attack on Bahrain, the line-up for APEC week in Shenzhen and the fifth death from the CFB Wainwright fire.

Ongoing stories — the ground stop and the New Orleans river collision — carry their original and updated dates. Reports that the U.S. has lost measles-elimination status were not repeated: the latest coverage still rests on unnamed sources, and the formal announcement is planned for Nov. 17.

Items described as planned or scheduled — the Grey Cup and the Snowbirds’ final flypast, the APEC CEO and leaders’ meetings, and the police facial-recognition rollout — are not presented as having happened.

This edition has photos on the lead and on 21 of 23 other stories, using only Wikimedia Commons or U.S. government public-domain files, each credited. All but one are file photos that do not show the events described; the Eurovision Asia picture was taken at the contest.

Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 4, World 5. China has four because several candidate stories were only available from the South China Morning Post, which blocked automated access this morning.
provenance: Stories are compiled from the linked sources; labels describe the type of claim each story rests on.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:17 and 6:20 AM ET; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.
CGTN and Xinhua (carried by RTHK) are Chinese state media and are labelled State media; RTHK is Hong Kong’s public broadcaster.
Some pages (the South China Morning Post and ESPN) returned access errors to automated fetches; those are access limits, not evidence that the reporting is wrong, and they are not cited.
Where outlets gave different figures — injuries in the Jordan church attack, and whether Italy’s Meta fine is its largest ever — the edition states both.

stories.headline: SpaceX catches a Starship spacecraft returning from orbit for the first time, after losing the booster
stories.deck: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with the launch tower’s mechanical arms in Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, about 22 hours after liftoff. The Super Heavy booster, which SpaceX had also hoped to catch, aborted and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico on Friday.
stories.summary: SpaceX caught the upper stage of its Starship rocket with the launch tower’s mechanical arms in Starbase, Texas, on Saturday, about 22 hours after liftoff. The Super Heavy booster, which SpaceX had also hoped to catch, aborted and exploded over the Gulf of Mexico on Friday. The 124-metre (407-foot) rocket lifted off from Starbase on Friday afternoon on its 15th full-scale test flight, the first in which SpaceX tried to recover both stages. Minutes after launch the booster triggered an automated abort and diverted to the ocean, where it exploded; Elon Musk said it had been “slightly low on fuel,” the BBC reported. The ship went on to deploy 26 Starlink satellites, circled Earth 14 times and then flew back to the tower, where the “chopsticks” arms caught it. SpaceX said the spacecraft, including its heat shield, appeared to work well, according to NPR. NASA, which is paying SpaceX to use Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon, welcomed the result. SpaceX had already caught boosters three times on earlier flights.
stories.why: A rocket whose two stages can both be flown again is what would make Starship cheap enough for moon landings, huge satellite launches and Musk’s Mars plans. Catching the spacecraft is the harder half of that goal, but the lost booster shows the full system still isn’t routine.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Duffy ties the nationwide ground stop to contractor work replacing copper wiring, but the FAA says the root cause is still unknown
stories.deck: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s nationwide ground stop followed upgrade work by contractor L3Harris to switch air traffic control communications from copper wire to fibre, after a router flooded other equipment with connection attempts. The FAA said flight schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday.
stories.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Friday’s nationwide ground stop followed upgrade work by contractor L3Harris to switch air traffic control communications from copper wire to fibre, after a router flooded other equipment with connection attempts. The FAA said flight schedules should be back to normal by the end of Sunday. At a Saturday news conference, Duffy said a router at “at least” one remote site sent more than 1,000 connection attempts roughly every five seconds, disrupting radio and radar feeds, CNBC reported. He said investigators were trying to determine whether the cause was “incompetence” — an installation error — or a faulty router. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said there was “zero evidence” of anything nefarious, that no FAA facility went dark, and that the agency grounded flights because it could not explain the instability; CNBC reported that the root cause had not been pinned down. L3Harris said it is supporting the FAA investigation and has completed more than 70% of the copper-to-fibre conversion. The BBC, citing flight-tracking data, said more than 15,000 U.S. flights were delayed or cancelled on Friday and more than 5,900 cancelled and 7,000 delayed on Saturday.
stories.why: Officials had first blamed old equipment; now the spotlight is on the work meant to replace it. Who is found responsible — the contractor, the hardware or the FAA’s own oversight — will shape the fight in Congress over the billions Duffy wants to modernize air traffic control.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Ongoing story first reported in the Nov 14 edition. The cause is the administration’s account so far; the FAA said the root cause had not been established. Flight counts are flight-tracking tallies cited by the BBC.

stories.headline: Judge temporarily blocks Trump’s plan to close a historic Washington public golf course for a 15-month rebuild
stories.deck: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order on Saturday, a day before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close for President Trump’s planned redevelopment into a championship-level course.
stories.summary: U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes issued a temporary restraining order on Saturday, a day before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close for President Trump’s planned redevelopment into a championship-level course. NPR said the order delays any work at the site for two weeks. The challenge was brought in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers, who argue the plan would change the character of the public course and make it unaffordable; Trump denies that. In her 30-page ruling, the BBC reported, Reyes wrote that the government’s justifications were pretextual, that it had violated at least two federal laws “to meet an arbitrary deadline,” and that closing a park “daily enjoyed by Washingtonians of all stripes” ran against the public interest. She also said the administration could not close the park or course but was not required to actively manage them. Trump had announced on Oct. 26 that the course would close on Nov. 15. The BBC said it had asked the White House for comment.
stories.why: The ruling tests how far a president can remake federal parkland around the capital on his own timetable. For now, a 106-year-old public course stays open while the case proceeds.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: Port of New Orleans sues the tanker’s owners over the cruise-boat collision, and a judge lets federal officials take control of the ship
stories.deck: The port says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt caused at least $1 million in damage when it struck the docked river cruise boat American Heritage on Friday, and alleges negligence by its owner and managers. A judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the ship for now.
stories.summary: The port says the tanker Atlantic Asphalt caused at least $1 million in damage when it struck the docked river cruise boat American Heritage on Friday, and alleges negligence by its owner and managers. A judge issued a warrant giving federal officials control of the ship for now. The lawsuit, filed Friday in federal court in the Eastern District of Louisiana, names the tanker, its owner Nave Shipping SA and manager Thome Ship Management, and asks that the vessel be seized and sold to cover the damage, the BBC reported. CBC, citing the Associated Press, said the tanker is owned by a subsidiary of a Chinese company. Everyone aboard survived; 32 people were taken to hospital with non-critical injuries and eight were still in hospital on Saturday. A Coast Guard captain said there appeared to have been “some type of a loss of steering.” The National Transportation Safety Board has recovered the tanker’s voyage data recorder and expects a preliminary report within 30 days. The cruise boat remains on its side against the terminal, and moving it could take weeks.
stories.why: Holding the tanker in port keeps a foreign-owned ship within reach of U.S. courts while investigators work out why it lost control on one of the country’s busiest rivers.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + allegation
stories.note: Ongoing story first reported in the Nov 14 edition. The negligence claims are the port’s allegations in its lawsuit and have not been tested in court.

stories.headline: Delray Beach cancels its nearly 60-year-old St. Patrick’s Day parade, citing Florida’s new anti-DEI law
stories.deck: The South Florida city said a state law that bars taxpayer money from diversity initiatives, taking effect Jan. 1, rules out city-sponsored celebrations of culture or heritage. It is also withdrawing its sponsorship of June Pride events.
stories.summary: The South Florida city said a state law that bars taxpayer money from diversity initiatives, taking effect Jan. 1, rules out city-sponsored celebrations of culture or heritage. It is also withdrawing its sponsorship of June Pride events. The city attorney advised that government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that aren’t national holidays could run afoul of the law, and Mayor Tom Carney said he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city’s biggest events, NPR reported. The parade has wound through downtown Delray Beach every year since 1970. Gov. Ron DeSantis, who backed the law, has called DEI initiatives discriminatory.
stories.why: It is an early, concrete sign of how broadly local officials may read Florida’s anti-DEI rules — reaching even a long-running Irish heritage parade, not only programs aimed at race or gender.

stories.headline: Alouettes and Elks set to meet in the 113th Grey Cup in Calgary, where the Snowbirds’ Tutor jets are due to fly for the last time
stories.deck: Montreal, the CFL’s best regular-season team, faces Edmonton at McMahon Stadium on Sunday. The Canadian Forces Snowbirds are scheduled to fly over the stadium at about 5 p.m. as part of the festivities before their CT-114 Tutor jets are retired.
stories.summary: Montreal, the CFL’s best regular-season team, faces Edmonton at McMahon Stadium on Sunday. The Canadian Forces Snowbirds are scheduled to fly over the stadium at about 5 p.m. as part of the festivities before their CT-114 Tutor jets are retired. The Alouettes went 14-4 and beat Winnipeg 33-23 in the East final; the Elks went 13-5 and beat B.C. 28-16 in the West final, The Canadian Press reported. Montreal lost last year’s Grey Cup to Saskatchewan; Edmonton is in its first Grey Cup since 2015, when the team was known as the Eskimos. Elks quarterback Cody Fajardo was Grey Cup MVP for Montreal in 2023. The Tutors, ordered as training aircraft in 1961, flew with the Snowbirds for 55 years; their replacements are not expected until the 2030s at the earliest, CBC reported.
stories.why: Canada’s biggest single-day sports event doubles this year as a farewell to a national symbol — and the gap until new jets arrive means the Snowbirds may be out of the sky for years.
stories.label: Reported
stories.note: The game and flypast are scheduled for Sunday, Nov 15; results were not available when this edition was prepared.

stories.headline: A fifth soldier dies of injuries from last month’s CFB Wainwright training-area fire
stories.deck: Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco of 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died Friday in an Ontario hospital, the Department of National Defence said.
stories.summary: Pte. William Douglas Dal Bianco of 3rd Battalion, Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry, died Friday in an Ontario hospital, the Department of National Defence said. The grass fire, which started during live-fire training on Oct. 17 and was driven by strong winds, initially killed four people. The Canadian Armed Forces said 38 personnel were injured in total; 24 were still in hospital and 14 had been released as of Saturday, the BBC reported. Prime Minister Mark Carney, Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre offered condolences.
stories.why: The death toll is still rising nearly a month on, with two dozen soldiers in hospital — keeping pressure on the military to explain how a training fire turned so deadly.

stories.headline: Carney says he will join the APEC “family photo” with Putin in Shenzhen, out of respect for host Xi Jinping
stories.deck: Speaking in Manila, the prime minister said Canada’s opposition to Russia is shown through sanctions and other policy, not by boycotting a group photo at next week’s summit.
stories.summary: Speaking in Manila, the prime minister said Canada’s opposition to Russia is shown through sanctions and other policy, not by boycotting a group photo at next week’s summit. “Yes, I will participate in the photo out of respect for the host. We’re in Asia,” Carney said, CBC reported. He pointed to Ottawa’s move to keep Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials out of next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta and said Canada stands “firmly with Ukraine.” Last month Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand chose to skip a G20 ministerial group photo with Russia’s Sergey Lavrov. The APEC leaders’ meeting is scheduled for later this week in Shenzhen, China; U.S. President Donald Trump is also expected to attend.
stories.why: Standing in the same frame as Putin is a small but visible concession; Carney is betting that good relations with Beijing matter more right now than the symbolism.

stories.headline: Hong Kong airport says runway-painting robots have cut line-marking time by more than half
stories.deck: The Airport Authority said Hong Kong International Airport is the first in the world to use robots to repaint airfield markings, a job they took on in September after a year of testing.
stories.summary: The Airport Authority said Hong Kong International Airport is the first in the world to use robots to repaint airfield markings, a job they took on in September after a year of testing. stories.headline: Scientists in Yunnan describe a giant hand-shaped fungus so distinct it forms a new family
stories.deck: Researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany named the species Dianjunus rex, after the ancient Dian Kingdom. Its fruiting bodies grow up to about 50 cm (20 inches) tall and weigh nearly 2.3 kg (5 lb), WIRED reported.
stories.summary: Researchers from the Kunming Institute of Botany named the species Dianjunus rex, after the ancient Dian Kingdom. Its fruiting bodies grow up to about 50 cm (20 inches) tall and weigh nearly 2.3 kg (5 lb), WIRED reported. The team found the whitish growths in soil near the roots of dying trees in the Nanban tropical rainforest. The fungus belongs to the Ascomycetes, the largest fungal phylum, and has no known close relatives. About 6,000 fungal species have been documented in Yunnan, but mycologists think the province could hold 100,000.
stories.why: A find this large going unnoticed until now shows how much of the living world is still undocumented — even in a well-studied corner of China.

stories.headline: Italy fines Meta €805 million for accessing Android users’ photos through Facebook without specific consent
stories.deck: Italy’s data protection authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million Android users that a Facebook feature suggesting posts from their phone galleries gave it access to their photos and videos. Meta says it will appeal.
stories.summary: Italy’s data protection authority said Meta did not properly inform about 20 million Android users that a Facebook feature suggesting posts from their phone galleries gave it access to their photos and videos. Meta says it will appeal. The regulator gave Meta 60 days to turn the camera-roll suggestion feature off by default and ask for consent separately, the BBC reported. DW said the fine equals 0.4% of Meta’s annual turnover and is the largest an Italian regulator has imposed on a big tech company; the BBC described it as among the largest. The authority also cited “Meta’s lack of co-operation.” Meta told the BBC it “strongly” disagrees with the assessment and called the fine disproportionate.
stories.why: European regulators keep using privacy law to set limits on how apps use what is on your phone. If the order holds, Facebook users in Italy will have to opt in before the app can scan their photos for suggestions.
